reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents its own BitClub Network opportunity as requiring viewers to join plans and contribute money in exchange for asserted cryptocurrency-mining compensation, with benefits conditioned on helping the club grow. Although it includes a risk disclaimer, the claimed mining operations, terms, compensation history, and production are described as unverified.

citations.quote: Tonight you are going to see a business proposal that is based, or, let's say, supported, by Big Dude Network which is a mining club

depending on your investment capacity you enter some of those plans that later we will leave and that money that you the money you contribute to the club, as a way to take part in those plans, the club invests into Iceland, mining robots, machines that make bitcoin
we simply invest and give them them to do the complicated part and we receive the production of these machines daily, that produces, this particular produces Bitcoin.
from $599 you can go to the club

opening.argument: The presentation openly qualifies its claims instead of offering a guaranteed outcome. It warns that cryptocurrency investing can cause partial or total loss and tells viewers to use only money they can afford to risk. It also rejects the idea of guaranteed, permanent results. That language is inconsistent with a deceptive promise of certainty: the audience is expressly told to evaluate risk and accept that the opportunity is not magic. The warning is reinforced visually by a slide headed “ADVERTENCIA” that repeats the possibility of partial or total loss. On this record, the speaker is presenting a speculative opportunity with an explicit caution, which supports treating the material as an anti-overclaiming promotion rather than scam content.

citations.quote: investing in cryptos involves partial risks or totals of lost money please you must participate only with summaries that each one of you can afford to risk
If you are a person who is looking for guarantee and permanent things, we believe that does not exist

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats the existence of a paid mining proposal as proof of deception, but its quotes establish only that the speaker describes participation and machines. They do not show a guaranteed return, concealment of risk, or a promise that viewers cannot lose money. The presentation expressly says the opposite: loss is possible and guarantees do not exist. The prosecution’s assertion that the operations are “unverified” is also not evidence that the claims are false.

citations.quote: investing in cryptos involves partial risks or totals of lost money please you must participate only with summaries that each one of you can afford to risk
If you are a person who is looking for guarantee and permanent things, we believe that does not exist

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A disclaimer does not neutralize the underlying solicitation. The video still describes money contributed to plans, machines producing Bitcoin, and production received by participants. Saying loss is possible merely acknowledges investment risk; it does not substantiate the claimed mining operation or compensation. The warning therefore limits the promise but does not establish that the paid opportunity is genuine.

citations.quote: the money you contribute to the club, as a way to take part in those plans, the club invests into Iceland, mining robots, machines that make bitcoin
we receive the production of these machines daily, that produces, this particular produces Bitcoin.

opening.argument: The format and stated purpose support an educational interpretation. The speaker calls the event a conference full of information, tells viewers that the recording can be reviewed, and says the goal is to put the project information in their hands so they can analyze it. The discussion explains mining, blockchain, decentralization, machines, and how the club is presented to operate. It even describes blockchain as a way to verify whether mining activity is recorded, rather than asking viewers to rely solely on trust. A tutorial or business-technology explanation can discuss an opportunity without becoming proof that the video itself is scam content. The available evidence shows an instructional presentation about a crypto project, not an independently established fraudulent outcome.

citations.quote: Today I have a conference full of information
all this conference will be recorded in this link
my only goal right now is sharing the information
the Blockchain is like the accounting book for everything that happens with bitcoin

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling something a conference does not make it education rather than promotion. The speaker expressly calls it a “business proposal,” presents plans tied to investment capacity, and identifies a $599 entry point. Those are not merely neutral explanations of blockchain. Still, the prosecution must show that the promotional claims are deceptive; describing a paid opportunity and explaining its mechanics does not by itself establish that.

citations.quote: Tonight you are going to see a business proposal
depending on your investment capacity you enter some of those plans
from $599 you can go to the club

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The educational framing cannot overcome the presentation’s direct call to join a paid mining plan. The speaker says viewers contribute money, receive daily production, and can enter from $599. Explaining blockchain or offering a recording does not verify that the promised machines, terms, or returns exist. The instructional format is therefore the vehicle for promoting the unverified paid opportunity, not evidence against scam classification.

citations.quote: the money you contribute to the club, as a way to take part in those plans
we receive the production of these machines daily
from $599 you can go to the club

opening.argument: The proposal can be read as ordinary participation in a club-operated service: members contribute toward plans, while the club handles the complicated infrastructure of mining. The speaker describes practical burdens such as configuration, internet, and heating, and says the club takes care of that work. Crucially, the material does not show a guaranteed return, a request for credentials, or a requirement to recruit a downline. It says that if someone invites nobody, nothing is taken from them and they are not punished. That is materially different from a coercive recruitment scheme. The evidence supports a paid service or business promotion whose safety cannot be certified, but ordinary promotion alone does not prove scam content.

citations.quote: You must take care of configuration, internet, heating, and many different things
we simply invest and give them them to do the complicated part
If you do not invite to anyone, nothing happens. They do not take anything from you, they do not punish you
this is not a sect or anything else, it is a legit mining club

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution’s own framing identifies a paid service, but labels it scam based on inference rather than a shown mechanism. The cited material does not establish a guaranteed return, mandatory recruitment, credential theft, or an outcome in which participants lose money. A compensation plan and optional invitations may be promotional features, yet the quoted evidence says participation does not require inviting anyone or incur punishment for declining. The case remains an unverified commerce claim, not demonstrated fraud.

citations.quote: If you do not invite to anyone, nothing happens. They do not take anything from you, they do not punish you
it is a very good opportunity but it is not magic

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of credential theft or explicit punishment is beside the point. The relevant mechanism is paid participation in a mining plan in exchange for asserted cryptocurrency production. The speaker states that money is contributed, machines supposedly produce Bitcoin, and participants receive that production. Calling invitations voluntary does not verify the mining, the contract, or the claimed compensation, so ordinary-commerce framing understates the central paid-return claim.
